summary: Introduces a syntax for defining feature sets formed from combinations and relations involving individual media features, such as saying a device supports one thing and either of two others. It was updated by RFC 2738 and RFC 2938.

eli5.summary: This is a way of writing rules like color and either big or small paper, so a device can describe its abilities in one neat sentence.

questions: how to describe device capabilities with feature sets
what is a media feature set
how does feature set matching work
what is a quality value in content negotiation
how to write a feature set predicate
subtitle: A compact Boolean syntax for saying which media features a sender, receiver or file format can handle, and a way to match two such descriptions.

tldr.problem: Protocols that negotiate content need a way to describe the combinations of media features that a sender, a recipient or a file format can handle, not just single features.
tldr.mechanism: A feature set is written as a Boolean predicate over feature tags, in a syntax modelled on LDAP search filters, such as (& (dpi>=150) (papersize=iso-A4)). Two descriptions are matched by converting their combination to disjunctive normal form and checking whether any conjunction can be satisfied.
tldr.outcome: The same expression style describes senders, receivers and file formats, and the matching algorithm finds what they have in common. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 2738 and RFC 2938.

today: RFC 2533 is a Proposed Standard published in March 1999. It has been updated by RFC 2738 and RFC 2938, so those documents should be read alongside it.

sections.title: The Need for Feature Set Descriptions
sections.content:
Many Internet application protocols need content negotiation. Part of any such framework is a way to describe the range of media features that the sender, the recipient or the transmission format of a message can handle. A separate memo, RFC 2506, supplies the vocabulary of individual media features and the registration procedure.

This memo adds a syntax for feature sets built from combinations and relations involving individual features, plus an algorithm for matching feature sets. The design treats feature set predicates as mathematical relations that put constraints on what can be handled. That lets one form of expression describe senders, receivers and file formats alike. It is loosely modelled on how relational databases use Boolean expressions, and the syntax is based on LDAP search filters.
sections.eli5: Before two machines swap a picture, each says what it can handle. This memo gives them one common way to say it.

sections.title: Collections, Sets and Predicates
sections.content:
A feature collection is a set of media feature tags with associated values. It can describe one specific rendering of one document by one recipient. A feature set is a set of zero, one or more feature collections. A feature set predicate is a function of a feature collection that returns a Boolean result. TRUE means the collection belongs to the set of capabilities that the predicate defines.

Feature values are simple atomic values: Booleans, enumerated values, text strings (treated like enumerated tokens) and numbers (integer or rational). All of them can be compared for equality, and numeric and ordered values can also be compared with <= and >=.

The general approach is to start from the assumption that anything is possible, then apply constraints that progressively remove document instances. A monochrome printer removes everything that uses colour, for example. Combining constraints is the logical AND of their predicates.

Within one feature collection, each feature tag may have only one value. The RFC stresses this in section 7.2, and it matters for how expressions are reduced.
sections.eli5: Imagine a huge box of every possible picture. Each rule throws out the pictures a device cannot show, and what is left is what the device can handle.

sections.title: The Textual Syntax
sections.content:
The text form comes from the LDAP search filter syntax of RFC 2254, keeping only what is relevant and adding quality values. The grammar is written in the ABNF of RFC 2234. A filter is a parenthesised component followed by optional ;parameter items.

  • (& f1 f2 ... fn) is the logical AND of the filters.
  • (| f1 f2 ... fn) is the logical OR.
  • (! f1) is the negation of a filter.
  • (ftag=value), (ftag<=value) and (ftag>=value) compare a named feature with a value.

Less-than and greater-than tests on non-numeric values amount to equality tests, because this specification defines no ordering for them. A set shorthand such as (paper-size=[A4,B4]) or (width=[4..17/2]) can combine enumerated values and ranges. It is only shorthand and is rewritten into plain comparisons.

Preferences are expressed with numeric quality values from 0 to 1 with up to 3 fractional digits, written ;q=0.8. Higher is preferred and equal values are equally preferred. The default is 1. Parameters may be attached to any filter, but only top-level quality values are recognized. The RFC gives no rules for combining preference information from different parts of an expression.
sections.eli5: The rules are written as little bracketed sentences. They say AND, OR or NOT, and compare a feature with a number or a word. A tiny score from 0 to 1 can show which choice you like best.

sections.title: Feature Values and Units
sections.content:
A feature value is a Boolean, number, token or string. Booleans are the tokens TRUE and FALSE, in any mix of letter case. A number is a decimal integer with an optional sign or a rational written n/m, so 3/2, +15/10 and 600/400 all mean 1.5. A sign must come before the whole rational, so 3/+2 is not valid. A token is letters, digits and hyphens, and a string is quoted text that is treated like a token.

Every feature tag has a standard unit, and a value in that unit carries no designation. If the standard resolution unit is dpcm, then (res=200) means 200 dots per centimetre and (res=72dpi) could mean 72 dots per inch. During matching, comparisons with different unit designators are treated as different features, so applications should adopt a consistent unit for each feature.

Feature values whose comparison rules are not covered, such as multi-part version strings, are outside this memo.
sections.eli5: Values can be yes or no, numbers, fractions or plain words. If you want to use a different unit, like inches instead of centimetres, you attach its name to the number.

sections.title: Matching Two Feature Sets
sections.content:
Testing a single feature collection against a predicate is easy: evaluate the predicate. The harder question is whether two feature sets overlap, for example whether a file format and a recipient share any feature collection. The RFC turns this into asking whether the combined predicate (& P Q) describes a non-empty set.

Because one feature tag can appear in several tests, the tests are not independent, so the predicates are reduced to a canonical disjunctive normal form: an outer OR of ANDs of possibly negated simple tests. The strategy is:

  1. Replace set expressions with plain comparisons.
  2. Move negations inwards using De Morgan's laws, then remove them by turning every comparison into just four relational operators, LE, GE, NL and NG.
  3. Expand into disjunctive normal form.
  4. For each conjunction, group tests by feature tag and merge them using the RFC's simplification rules for ordered and unordered values. A contradiction means that conjunction can never be satisfied and is discarded.
  5. If at least one conjunction survives, the feature sets overlap, and the surviving expression can be used for further matching.

Picking a final choice from the matches, by quality values or otherwise, is not covered here.
sections.eli5: To see if two lists of abilities overlap, you combine them and cross out any combination that argues with itself, like needing both red and not red. If anything is left, the two can work together.

sections.title: Named and Auxiliary Predicates
sections.content:
A named predicate gives a name and optional formal parameters to a reusable expression, written (fname pname...) :- filter. The only mechanism this memo defines to introduce one is an auxiliary predicate: a where ... end block attached to a filter. The named predicates are visible in the filter body but not from each other, and recursion is not permitted.

For matching, each invocation is replaced by the predicate body, with formal parameters replaced by the actual ones, before conversion to normal form. Without recursion this is guaranteed to terminate. The RFC restates its resolution example with an auxiliary predicate named Res to avoid repeating the list of resolution pairs three times.
sections.eli5: If you keep writing the same long list, you can give it a nickname and use the nickname instead.

sections.title: A Worked Fax Example
sections.content:
The RFC matches a high-end black-and-white fax receiver against a document that is available in three formats. The receiver is described by (& (dpi=[200,300]) (grey=2) (color=0) (image-coding=[MH,MR])). The document is the OR of a 300 dpi bi-level MR version, a 200 dpi bi-level version coded MH or MMR, and a 300 dpi colour JPEG version.

After expanding, distributing and grouping by feature tag, only two conjunctions survive: 300 dpi with MR coding, and 200 dpi with MH coding. The colour version drops out because the receiver cannot handle colour or JPEG. The 300 dpi version must be sent with MR coding, because the RFC says this is the only coding of the image data that the receiver can use for high resolution documents.

Section 7.2 adds a warning about tag scoping. Because a tag has one value per collection, using stripe-size with both 256 and 128 in one expression makes that conjunction false. The fix is separate feature tags such as MRC-stripe-size and JBIG-stripe-size.
sections.eli5: A fax machine only likes black and white, so the colour copy is thrown out. Only two black-and-white choices work for both sides, and the sender can pick either.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists primary concerns for capability identification: unintentional disclosure of private information through announced capabilities or preferences, disruption caused by accidental or malicious incorrect capability information, and use of capability data to probe a network and exploit known weaknesses of specific hosts.

Mechanisms that automatically send capability data in response to a query from an unknown system are the most contentious. Directory services based on LDAP seem less problematic because proper authentication is available. Format-converting gateways may also be problematic, since they tend to defeat message integrity and authenticity checks.
sections.eli5: Telling everyone exactly what your device can do can give away private details, and wrong information can cause trouble, so be careful who you tell and who you believe.

items.title: LE
items.text: a is less than or equal to b.

items.title: GE
items.text: a is greater than or equal to b.

items.title: NL
items.text: Not less: the negation of LE.

items.title: NG
items.text: Not greater: the negation of GE.
